newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS - East European bourses mixed in quiet trading.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - East European bourses mixed in quiet trading.

text.p: East European stock exchanges traded mixed this week, with Warsaw rising slightly, Prague easing because of a banking crisis and Budapest weakening on international news.
Croatian and Slovenian stocks rose, while Bratislava shares eased, Bucharest and Tirana had no trades and investors focused on foreign currency and treasury papers in Bulgaria.
WARSAW
Polish shares rose this week but analysts said the market could be entering a sideways trend, starting a typical consolidation period after rising for much of September.
The WIG index closed at 14,735.5 points, up 1.6 percent from last Friday's close.

Analysts said Friday's news that food prices grew 1.3 percent in September's second third meant it was still possible that year-on-year inflation would end the month lower than 20 percent and lay the ground for a possible interest-rate cut.
BUDAPEST
Budapest bourse prices were driven by international developments, primarily news about Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health and by expectations of a U.S. rate hike.
With U.S. Fed rates unchanged, the BUX index began to rise on Thursday after two losing sessions. On Friday, it closed at 3,547.37 points, down 2.83 from last Friday.
PRAGUE
Czech shares continued to suffer from the fallout of a recent banking crisis for most of the week, though a blue chip surge on Thursday brought with it hopes for the beginning of a market turnaround.
The PX50 index fell 7.9 points on the week to close on Friday at 557.9.
The PSE had lost just over five percent after Kreditni Banka's failure led to the fifth biggest Czech bank, Agrobanka, being put under forced administration last week.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava exchange saw a week of listless trading, with significantly smaller volumes of shares generally traded in the Slovak blue chips.
The 12-share SAX index dipped during the week, from Monday's open at 208.68 points to Friday's close at 202.55 points.
Market analysts did not expect the market to recover from its current apathy over the next few weeks.
BULGARIA
Only two corporate issues traded on the Bulgarian stock market this week as investors sought more liquid investments, including foreign currency and treasury paper.
Weekly repo turnover rose to an all-time high of 23.619 million levs from 3.54 million the week before and a previous record of 16.2 billion two months ago, due to a record high main interest rate.
Treasury paper became an attraction after the Bulgarian National Bank raised its central interest rate to an annual 300 percent from 108 percent, effective Tuesday.
Total stock turnover amounted to 15,550 levs and traded volume was 400 stocks.
The 13-share Reuter All Bulgaria Stock Index (RABSI) closed at 41.02 points on Friday, down 0.12 on the week.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares rose 9.6 percent, fuelled by a strong performance of drug company Lek's A issue.
The SBI index firmed 88.39 points to 1,007.25.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks continued to rally amid new gains in leading issues with slight corrections, while market participants said the current bull run would last for a while.
The biggest gainer confectioner Kras jumped 60.50 kuna to 530.50. Fully-listed Zagrebacka Banka rose 100 kuna to a new high of 1,000, continuing a steady climb.
BUCHAREST
The Bucharest stock exchange was closed this week as it started to install new software to improve trading and settlement. It is due resume trading on October 1.
TIRANA
No treasury bills or state bonds changed hands in Tirana during its weekly sessions on Monday and Thursday.
